article.headline: The $1.1 Trillion Hallucination: What Ventuals' Anthropic Token Actually Measures
article.lede: A derivatives platform called Ventuals now lets anyone take leveraged bets on the implied valuation of Anthropic, which its perpetual-futures contract placed above $1.1 trillion in late April. That number is not a valuation. It is, at best, a sentiment reading dressed in the grammar of finance.
article.body:
To understand what the Ventuals "Anthropic token" represents, it helps to start with what it does not. It confers no ownership stake in Anthropic PBC. It carries no voting rights, no claim on future cash flows, no priority in any hypothetical liquidation. What it does is allow a trader — using up to twenty times leverage — to speculate on whether a number derived from infrequent, illiquid, minority-share transactions in the secondary market will go up or down. The contract is a perpetual futures instrument, which means it has no expiry date and is settled continuously in a dollar-pegged stablecoin called USDH, with positions marked to a synthetic index rather than to any underlying asset. In plain language: you are not buying a sliver of Anthropic; you are placing a bet about what people in an opaque market will later be willing to pay for a sliver of Anthropic.

Ventuals launched in 2025 on Hyperliquid's on-chain order-book infrastructure, following the HIP-3 standard for builder-deployed perpetuals. Its markets denominate contracts in "Valuation Units" — a company's total implied valuation divided by one billion, so that a mark of 1,114 translates to $1.114 trillion. The oracle that produces that mark is a hybrid: fifty percent off-chain data sourced from institutions including Notice (which aggregates funding-round valuations, secondary-market transaction quotes, and 409A assessments — the last being the internal appraisals companies conduct for tax purposes and employee equity pricing) and fifty percent on-chain from Hyperliquid's own eight-hour exponential moving average of the futures price itself. That reflexive loop — where the futures price partly anchors the oracle that prices the futures — is not a glitch in the design. It is the design. It allows the market to "price in" information that no single secondary-market transaction has formally confirmed, but it also means the contract can drift arbitrarily far from any real-world transaction price when speculative momentum overwhelms the off-chain anchor.

The structural fragility in this setup is not subtle. Secondary markets for private-company shares — platforms like Forge Global and Caplight, which aggregate bids and offers from accredited investors — are themselves thin, illiquid, and based on minority positions that carry no governance rights. A trade of, say, $5 million in Anthropic common stock on Forge does not "value" Anthropic at $1 trillion any more than a single house sale on a quiet cul-de-sac establishes the value of every home in a city. Those marks update infrequently; the Ventuals oracle acknowledges explicitly that "private market valuations are updated infrequently, which may result in delayed price anchoring." When leveraged futures traders are able to move the on-chain component of the oracle, the mark can decouple from even those thin reference transactions. Anthropic's most recent formal funding round, a $30 billion Series G closed in February 2026 at a post-money valuation of $380 billion, is already less than a third of where Ventuals placed the contract by late April — a divergence of the kind that would be embarrassing on any regulated exchange.

Anthropicʼs underlying business has been genuinely extraordinary by almost any measure. Annualised revenue grew from roughly $9 billion at end-2025 to $30 billion by March 2026, driven by enterprise adoption of Claude Code and the company's API layer — a 233 percent increase in a single quarter. That trajectory, if it holds, would justify a very high multiple. But "very high" and "three times the Series G post-money valuation within ten weeks" are different claims. The first is a reasonable extrapolation from observable data; the second is the kind of figure that emerges when retail traders with twenty-times leverage discover a narrative they like. The open interest on the Ventuals Anthropic contract sat at roughly $5.6 million as of the screenshots in question — small enough that even a few coordinated or momentum-driven positions can swing the mark materially.

Stefan Schubert, a philosopher and moral psychologist at the London School of Economics who studies the psychology of effective altruism and contributed a book on the subject with Oxford University Press in 2025, observed simply that the number "keeps rising" and had "more than doubled in three weeks." That is accurate as a description of the chart. It also illustrates a peculiar feature of this asset class: in the absence of continuous fundamental data — Anthropic does not publish quarterly earnings; its valuation is re-anchored only at funding rounds — the price discovery process on Ventuals is less like a market and more like a Schelling point, a number that accrues gravity because enough participants believe others will believe it. The Ventuals chart for Anthropic running from a mark of $111 to $1,114 in a compressed timeframe is a picture of what perpetual futures mechanics produce when the underlying reference price is both sparse and lagged.

None of this makes Ventuals illegitimate as an experiment. Retail investors have long been excluded from pre-IPO exposure to companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX, and the demand for some form of participation — even synthetic, even leveraged, even detached from legal ownership — is real and comprehensible. What these instruments cannot do is substitute for that ownership. OpenAI made the point bluntly in a different context, noting that certain secondary structures "may carry no legal value" and that the company "treats them as void." Ventuals contracts are more modest in their claims, but the underlying problem is the same: you cannot construct a sound derivative on top of an opaque mark, leverage that derivative twenty times, and then read the resulting price as evidence of what a company is worth. The Anthropic token at $1.1 trillion tells you something about the mood of a small group of crypto-native traders in a thin, self-referential market. It tells you rather less about Anthropic.

concepts.definition: A derivative contract that tracks the price of an underlying asset and has no expiry date. Positions are continuously marked to market and settled through funding payments between longs and shorts. Unlike a conventional futures contract, there is no delivery date — and therefore no terminal anchor forcing the price to converge on any real-world transaction.

The total enterprise value imputed to a company by extrapolating from the price of a small number of minority-share transactions in secondary markets. Because private companies do not trade continuously and sellers of minority stakes lack control rights, implied valuations are highly sensitive to the terms of the last visible transaction and can diverge substantially from what a buyer would pay to acquire the whole company.

An on-chain perpetual-futures platform built on Hyperliquid's order-book infrastructure that allows traders to take leveraged positions on the implied valuations of private, pre-IPO companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX. Contracts are denominated in Valuation Units (a company's implied valuation divided by one billion) and settled in USDH, a dollar-pegged stablecoin. Ownership of a Ventuals position confers no equity stake in the underlying company.

article.fact_check: The Ventuals mark of $1.114 trillion for Anthropic as of late April 2026 is roughly three times the $380 billion post-money valuation from the February 2026 Series G funding round — Anthropic's most recent formal primary-market price anchor. The divergence is structurally predictable: the Ventuals oracle combines sparse secondary-market data with a reflexive on-chain component derived from the futures price itself, and with only $5.6 million in open interest the contract is thin enough for momentum to dominate fundamentals. Ventuals positions confer no ownership rights; a Ventuals mark is not equivalent to, and should not be compared directly with, primary-round post-money valuations or secondary-market share prices on regulated platforms such as Forge Global. The platform's own documentation acknowledges that 'private market valuations are updated infrequently, which may result in delayed price anchoring.' The rapid run-up — more than doubling in three weeks — is consistent with leveraged momentum trading on a thinly capitalised instrument, not with a genuine reappraisal of Anthropic's fundamental value.

poster_stefanfschubert.bio: Philosopher and moral psychologist. Research Fellow, London School of Economics. Co-author of 'Effective Altruism and the Human Mind: The Clash Between Impact and Intuition' (Oxford University Press, 2025, with Lucius Caviola). PhD in Philosophy, Lund University; MPhil Psychology, University of Cambridge; MSc Neuroscience, University College London. Previously: University of Oxford, Centre for Effective Altruism. Based in Stockholm, Sweden.
